https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/brit.title: Trustee quits British Museum over record £50m sponsorship deal with BP
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/brit.subtitle: Museum chiefs say deal is vital to renovate buildings and develop new galleries
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/brit.text:
The British Museum has lost its deputy chairwoman and believes it is facing an increased risk of violent attacks after doubling down on its relationship with the fossil fuel industry by striking a new £50 million sponsorship deal with BP.
The museum’s board has surprised the country’s cultural community by signing a ten-year deal with BP, which has in recent years been shunned by almost all of Britain’s artistic organisations.
It has emerged the board took the decision in June last year at a meeting in which they agreed to “operate as a united board” despite personal disagreements.
The minutes of the meeting, from which the chairman George Osborne withdrew after declaring a conflict of interest, record that “it was unanimously agreed that accepting the sponsorship was on balance in the best interests of the museum and the protection, display and use of its collection”.
Muriel Gray resigned her post at the meeting in November immediately before the trustees discussed how to make public the BP deal.
Gray, who had been a trustee for seven years, did not respond to requests on Tuesday for a comment. The minutes record Gray saying she had made a personal decision to submit her resignation to the government.
A fellow trustee, Dame Mary Beard, said last night that she had opposed the sponsorship deal when the board was asked to make a decision.
She said in an email: “I only have this to say. I accepted as a Board member the view of the majority of the Trustees (who I know looked long and hard at this). But it was not my view and speaking personally this would not have been my decision.”
Trustees were also warned about the increased risks of damage to its collection of priceless objects from protesters angered by the sponsorship deal. There were also concerns about the “personal safety of staff and trustees”.
BP and other oil and gas companies have been increasingly shunned by Britain’s cultural sector in recent years. The National Portrait Gallery, Royal Shakespeare Company and Tate are among those who have been cutting ties.
The deal highlights the difficulties artistic organisations have in raising money after 15 years of declining financial support from the state.
Chris Garrard, co-director of the pressure group, Culture Unstained, said that it was an “astonishingly out of touch and completely indefensible decision”.
“It comes just days after delegates at Cop28 agreed that the world must transition away from fossil fuels. We believe this decision is illegitimate and in breach of the museum’s own climate commitments and sector-wide codes and will be seeking legal advice in order to mount a formal challenge to it.”
Doug Parr, UK policy director for Greenpeace, said: “The arts and culture world has been steadily cutting ties with big oil, after realising the handy role they play in cleaning up their climate-wrecking image. Yet BP have wormed their way back into the British Museum with what must surely be one of the biggest, most brazen greenwashing sponsorship deals the sector has ever seen.”
The British Museum has released polling that it had commissioned suggesting that 59 per cent of the public were in favour of museums accepting donations from oil and gas companies and preferred corporate donations over taxpayers’ money.
The British Museum’s masterplan, which is expected to cost more than £1 billion, involves significant refurbishment, a new energy centre and archaeological research centre, as well as a revamp of many of its galleries.
It is due to launch an architectural competition to redevelop about 7,500 sq m of its gallery space including the galleries housing the collections of objects from Ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome.
Hartwig Fischer, the previous director of the museum, had spoken during his tenure about a renovation project similar to the Louvre’s projet grand, in which the French institution spent about £780 million, at 1993 prices, on a renovation.
Renovating the Western Range alone, with its Parthenon Sculptures, Rosetta Stone and countless other Mediterranean treasures, will take years, many partial gallery closures, and hundreds of millions of pounds.
Hartwig had also suggested the museum’s substantial holdings from under-represented regions of the world, such as Africa and South America, would be given more prominence as part of the masterplan.
The museum said on Tuesday that the “urgent need of renovation” of the grade I listed building made it necessary for trustees to seek “funding on this scale”.
There have been concerns about leaking roofs in the gallery housing the Parthenon Friezes, for example.
Charlie Mayfield, a trustee and chairman of the museum’s masterplan committee, said they were grateful to BP for their support. The company will be “credited as one of our valued sponsors”.
Mayfield added: “The British Museum is one of the largest and most visited cultural institutions in the world but some of its buildings are over 200 years old and in urgent need of refurbishment. That’s why the masterplan is so essential — and it’s exciting to be moving forward with our plans.”
He said that next year the museum would “begin the process of completely overhauling our outdated energy infrastructure and replacing it with state of the art facilities that will dramatically reduce our carbon footprint”.
Louise Kingham, BP’s senior vice-president, Europe, said: “The British Museum offers a window to the world for the millions of people that pass through its doors every year. As a business that has made Britain its home for over a century, we are proud to be a long-term partner to this important British institution and play our part in its future transformation — while helping to ensure that this iconic cultural venue remains freely accessible to all.”
If you are a security guard in search of an interesting job, I suggest you head straight to the British Museum. After this shock news, the galleries and gates of that vast institution in Bloomsbury will surely require a lot more protecting — for the next ten years at least.
That’s the duration of the £50 million sponsorship deal announced between the museum and BP. The oil giant used to be the biggest corporate sponsor of several top British arts organisations, including the Royal Opera House and the Royal Shakespeare Company. One by one they all dropped BP as pressure from anti-oil campaigners mounted.
Indeed, the campaign to force the arts world to cut all links with the fossil-fuel industry has reached such a peak that even getting sponsorship from finance houses with minor investments in oil companies is now seen in some quarters as morally reprehensible.
This was evident last summer when Greta Thunberg and 100 authors threatened a boycott of the Edinburgh Book Festival if it continued accepting money from the finance company Baillie Gifford, which had just 2 per cent of its investments in oil-related industries.
So the decision by George Osborne, the museum’s chairman, to accept £50 million from BP — the No 1 target on the Just Stop Oil hit-list — is bound to be inflammatory. In the past, anti-oil activists have deployed considerable ingenuity to infiltrate London’s top museums and galleries and enact headline-grabbing stunts. Their reaction to a deal of this size is sure to be angry and prolonged.
So why has the museum done it? The simple answer is that the masterplan to revitalise its venerable galleries and decaying infrastructure, first mooted a decade ago, hasn’t yet left the drawing board. The cost is likely to top a billion pounds, the government won’t foot the bill and BP made the museum an offer it simply couldn’t refuse.
This £50 million won’t cover more than a fraction of the cost, but the deal is psychologically important. It sends a message to other potential corporate sponsors and philanthropists that, however sniffy the rest of the cultural world is about accepting what it regards as “tainted” money, the British Museum is open for business with donors engaged in legitimate trades.
That approach deserves more support than one suspects it will get. The spectacle of famous actors and authors jetting round international festivals then demanding that arts organisations divest themselves of sponsorship from fossil-fuel companies is as hypocritical as it is impractical and hysterical. Pragmatically, it also won’t make a jot of difference to whether the world reaches its targets on carbon emissions. What it will do is bankrupt the arts and museum worlds, which are already perilously short of funds and still struggling to recapture their audiences after the disruption of the pandemic.
That said, I don’t envy the task awaiting the (yet to be appointed) new director of the British Museum. As if dealing with the Elgin Marbles controversy and the fallout from the mass theft of 2,000 objects from the museum’s collections is not enough, the likelihood of weekly disruption from protests could require the imposition of security measures more appropriate to a military base than a museum.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Feargal Sharkey: The fight for clean water is uniting the country
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
This was the year the water industry, agriculture, the regulators and the government promised to clean up their act. Clean rivers would be prioritised over profit.
This most precious resource would no longer be delivered at the expense of environmental degradation. Swimmers, paddlers, sailors and anglers would once again be able to enjoy the nation’s waterways free from unspeakable lurking pollutants, both invisible and all too obvious.
The most high-profile campaigner against river pollution has long been Feargal Sharkey, the singer turned environmental lobbyist. Have the authorities, I asked him this week, started to make good on their pledges? Or are England’s rivers as filthy as ever?
“To quote Johnny Rotten,” he says before he’s even got his coat off, having just bounced through the door of a north London pub where we met on Thursday night, “‘ever get the feeling you’ve been cheated?’”
The question is rhetorical. “My God, have we been cheated! Absolutely shafted. Seventy two billion paid in dividends! Sixty billion of debt! Nearly three million hours pumping out raw sewage in 2021! Three billion litres lost in leaks every day! Just 14 per cent of our rivers with “good” ecological status and every single one polluted to some extent. Studies say that will soon be down to 6 per cent without massive intervention.”
Sharkey tells interviewers he retired as a singer because he didn’t want to be an old rock star with “a receding hairline and a ponytail”. So he became, instead, a music industry executive, a lobbyist, a respected committee man and, latterly, a solo, wildly successful voice against river pollution, his Twitter account a clearing house for articles exposing the scandalous state of England’s water industry.
As Sharkey draws breath, I decide his joke about the getting into activism to avoid the fate of the fading star does not provide the full explanation of his apparent transformation. For one thing, at 65, he still has a magnificent head of hair, the fringe he sported on Top of the Pops back in the late Seventies still long and thick enough for him to have to continually flick it out of his eyes in a trademark gesture.
For another, two hours in his company is more than enough time (five minutes does the trick) to realise that this is man whose quick, clever mind, articulacy and command of detail were never going to be satisfied with a late middle-age spent recycling the hits of his youth.
For anyone under the impression he is a dilettante pop star turned eager yet amateurish campaigner, you could not be more wrong: Feargal Sharkey is one of the most intellectually impressive people I’ve interviewed in 30-plus years. This is a seriously bright man. He’s also entertaining, confident, with an unsparing line in invective.
“The people I meet in the water industry wouldn’t make it to lunchtime on Tuesday in the music business,” he says. “They’d be gone. Nobody would tolerate their level of incompetence.”
He feels the same way about the supposed regulators, Ofwat and the Environment Agency, and the elected ministers who sit above them.
“They’re mediocre, and that’s being polite. They cannot fend off one bloke in north London with nothing more than a f***ing mobile phone and a social media account. What does that say about their leadership qualities? They’re not up to it! After 13 years and countless reshuffles, we’re now not scraping the barrel, we’re drilling into the concrete the f***ing barrel is sitting on.”
The other factor behind Sharkey’s transition into such a compelling campaigner is that it’s not really a transition: he’s been doing it all his life. The second-youngest of seven, he was raised in Derry’s Bogside in a highly political household. His dad, Jim, was a radical but non-sectarian trade unionist and Labour Party stalwart; his mum, Sibeal, a classic indomitable Irish matriarch.
By the age of ten, in the late Sixties, young Feargal was already a veteran of the city’s civil rights marches with their demands to end institutionalised discrimination against Catholics in the province. In many ways, it was the interlude as a professional musician that was the aberration.
All that he’s done since calling time on performing in the Nineties — chairing government commissions, regulating commercial radio, effectively acting as the leading spokesman for Britain’s music industry for many years, now eviscerating the UK’s woeful water companies on a daily basis — is a return to the advocacy and activism with which he grew up.
He could have been a barrister, a politician, a mandarin. Exciting and melodic as the Undertones once were, I would trade that to have had Sharkey’s clarity and competence at the heart of UK governance these past four decades instead.
Never mind, he’s getting close to the centre of power now. A member of the Labour Party himself, Sharkey’s influence will be felt very clearly at Defra as and when his party forms a government. Will Labour come down in favour of renationalisation, I ask? His response is instructive. “There’s no decision. Is renationalisation the answer? I don’t know. Is the industry and its regulators in need of massive reform? Yes. After that we can get into a discussion of what [ownership] might look like. Right now I’m cautious. I wouldn’t take anything off the table.”
I say fair enough; perhaps renationalising an industry with £60 billion of debt is not ideal. “Listen,” he urges, leaning across the table and tapping my arm for emphasis: “I can think of lots of ways to nationalise them without it costing a penny. The new chairman of Thames Water told a parliamentary committee today that nationalisation would cost the taxpayer a pretty penny. That is a misleading and untrue statement.”
The trouble is (I’m paraphrasing, but not much) Sharkey and many other experts, not to mention consumers, think that after almost 34 years of mismanagement, assuming public ownership — in the manner of Northern Rock, or RBS — is too good for the water industry. “If you nationalise, even for nothing, you’ve let companies off the hook. Does the public want that? I recently spoke at a Financial Times event. The first questioner — a woman, well-spoken, turned out she was a KC — said: ‘Feargal: I need these people to feel pain’.”
“Why should the taxpayer,” he goes on, “be on the hook for fixing their sorry mess, which we’ve already paid for? The power is there to enforce the law! Always has been, section 19 of the 1991 Water Act: Ofwat can issue an enforcement order [over sewage releases] and if they don’t comply, it can fine them 10 per cent of their annual turnover.” The power is there, never been used!”
It is much the same story with agriculture, an even bigger river polluter, as a report from the centre-right think tank Onward showed when released on Saturday. “The ‘Farming Rules for Water’ are there, since 2003,” cries Sharkey. “They’re not enforced!” Environment Agency inspections of farms have been slashed, court cases barely pursued, dozens of videos circulate online of farmers spraying excess slurry over hedges into fields, soon to be washed into the nearest water course. Even so, “I’ve massive sympathy for farmers,” says Sharkey. “But some of our agriculture is unsustainable.”
If Sharkey sounds angry and animated, he is not alone. I’ve rarely known an issue as likely to enrage people — right across the political spectrum — as England’s polluted waterways. “The last time I got stopped in the street this much I had a number one record,” he confirms. I mention that I recently interviewed the Tory MP Danny Kruger, tribune of the rural, communitarian (some would say feudalistic) right, and he was every bit as livid as the most left-wing deep-green eco warrior about our rivers.
“I know Danny,” says Sharkey. “And I know where he’s coming from. And I know his mum [Prue Leith].” This illustrates Sharkey is no shouty Just Stop Oil-style radical. He’s an insider, well-connected in Whitehall and Westminster, willing and able to do the hard yards in the corridors and committee rooms of power. “Some call it selling out, I call it buying in.”
The received wisdom about Sharkey’s environmentalism is it originated in his lifelong love of fly-fishing. While the passion for angling is accurate, I suspect this is a man who, having spent many years championing live music and ensuring the legal framework existed for it to flourish, would have found another cause to fight soon enough even if he’d never picked up a fishing rod. Yet while the “genial Irish fella who just wants to cast for trout without wading through crap” narrative greatly underestimates Sharkey’s subtlety and sophistication, the raw outrage he feels owes a lot to the sheer pleasure of his chosen leisure pursuit.
“This week, the Atlantic salmon in the UK was added to the red list of endangered species. A species, been here since the last Ice Age, on the brink of extinction. What did Defra say? Nothing.” Sharkey has just stepped down after five years as chairman of the venerable Amwell Magna Fishery on the River Lea in Hertfordshire. But he’s still up there in his waders, every Sunday morning for a couple of hours at a minimum. “In 40 minutes from my home I can be standing in chalk stream to cast a dry fly at a wild brown trout born and bred in the biggest tributary of the River Thames. Pure tranquillity, as Izaak Walton said in The Compleat Angler, which was the predecessor of Gone Fishing now that I think about it, 400-odd years ago. I’ve got this lunatic mind going 50,000mph with 79 things going on. I can push all that noise to the back.” Does he catch much? “Most of the time. I’m quite good! But I’ve been doing it since I was ten.”
He brings a similar 55 years of experience to bear on excoriating the greed, lack of accountability, incompetence and absence of leadership which has resulted in England’s rivers swimming in shit. “I’ve always deployed the same strategy. Let’s have a grown up, pragmatic sit-down discussion. Here’s the problem, here’s the solution, here’s what I need you to do. If we’re clever everyone walks out with a big smile. All I want is a grown up, pragmatic response back. But if you don’t want to take that route, I know 1,000 other ways for you to end up where I want you to be.” I don’t doubt it.
Born August 13, 1958, Derry, Northern Ireland
Career As a teenager, started playing music with friends who would become the punk group The Undertones. Became their lead singer and in 1978, they were signed and released their hit debut single, Teenage Kicks. Became a solo singer in 1983. His song A Good Heart reached No 1 in 1985. In the Nineties, worked for Polydor Records and the Radio Authority, later became the head of UK Music. Appointed OBE for services to music in 2019. Now a campaigner and lobbyist for cleaner rivers and streams. Supported The Times Clean It Up campaign this year.
Family Lives in north London with his wife.
I’m a Celebrity or Strictly Come Dancing: “Neither! Strictly, under duress!”
Fish and chips or pan-fried turbot: “Fish and chips every time”.
Derry Girls or Normal People: “Derry Girls is brilliant, sublime comedy.”
The Nile or The Seine: “I’ve never been to the Nile but the Seine is disgusting.”
Spotify or SoundCloud: “At least Spotify pay the artist, miserable amount as it is.”
Guinness or G&T: “Vodka and Coke for me please.”
Uber or Lime: “Uber. I live at the top of a hill.”
Deadliest Catch or River Monsters: “River Monsters.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/obvi.title: John Vidal obituary
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/obvi.subtitle: Adventurous journalist who went native when he covered Swampy’s protests and was The Guardian’s first environment editor
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/obvi.text:
In 1996 John Vidal blagged his way into a job as a security guard at Newbury bypass, a road development that was swamped by activists, by disguising himself as a French carpenter.
“Frenchie”, as the guards called him, was in reality The Guardian’s first environment editor and he would have liked to have been hanging off the trees with the protesters he was supposed to be evicting. It was perhaps this — as well as the theatrical bursts of “non!” and “merde alors!” — that gave the game away when Vidal was escorted off the premises and told never to return.
When he inevitably did, he joined the tree-dwellers to tell their side of the story. They included Daniel Hooper, better known as “Swampy”, who became the unofficial figurehead of the environmental protest movement, at least as far as the national print and TV media was concerned.
Vidal had an indefatigable appetite for adventure. He breathed teargas in five countries — “Italian is the sweetest, American the worst” — and he camped down tunnels, across forests and in Michael Heseltine’s backyard as activists began to react to increasing ­ecological devastation at the turn of the century.
His first outing as a Frenchman was working undercover in a chicken slaughterhouse; he once fled Indonesia when his presence at a goldmine was noticed; and in 2009 he joined “shamans” at a crop-circle conference in Wiltshire — only to tag along, again undercover, with an expedition to build the circles that night, using ropes and planks of wood. His subsequent ­report did not go down well with the fake shamans.
In 1997 Vidal sailed with Greenpeace activists in a dinghy bound for Rockall, a small granite islet in the Atlantic Ocean, claimed by the UK, which had been licensed to 17 oil companies. “Twice the bolted-on ladder offers itself to the dinghy,” he wrote as they attempted landfall. “Twice we are swept out of reach. The third time, as two formidable waves sweep round from Rockall’s north and east flanks, we are lifted 20ft, right into the rock.”
In 1989 Vidal, then an arts critic for The Guardian, had suggested to Peter Preston, the paper’s editor, that they cover the fast-emerging climate issue in greater depth. It was the year that more than two million Britons voted Green in the European parliament elections, while James Hansen, a Nasa scientist, had warned the US Congress a year earlier about the consequences of a phenomenon called global warming.
Few people, he later wrote, were really listening. The nascent field of environmental journalism was swamped with dry graphs and numerical reports, and Vidal realised that to capture people’s imagination he needed to colour his causes into compelling ­stories. He saw climate change as “theatre on the world stage” (he had been a drama critic) and his articles were stitched with a rich cast of characters, such as protesters “disappearing into the mist”.
He was sceptical of power structures and the prevailing orthodoxy that big businesses, such as Shell and BP, were helping to tackle climate change with pledges of decarbonisation. By the same token he had an eye for “David and Goliath” stories, such as the ­Nigerian community which won a court settlement against Shell over decades of environmental abuse, or how Monsanto, one of the world’s largest seed companies, was putting small farmers out of business. He was selfless but never self-congratulatory: one of his proudest achievements was setting up the Gumbi Education Fund, a charity based in a poor village in Malawi.
In 1997 he covered the McLibel court case in which McDonald’s sued five Greenpeace activists over a pamphlet that accused the multinational of worker exploitation, animal cruelty, unhealthy food and environmental destruction. He wrote about it in depth in McLibel, with help from a barrister called Keir Starmer. A judge called it “obligatory reading for all responsible citizens”.
As his Guardian colleague ­George Monbiot said, Vidal shaped the nature of environmental journalism — even if he could be scatty and absent-minded. (He sometimes lost work he had commissioned from younger journalists and he was invariably late to things.)
In truth he was happiest travelling the world, and on his return, colleagues recalled him bounding fresh-faced into the office bearing exotic trinkets. When he joined Greenpeace on a month-long trip to the Arctic in 2012, he yelled his story down the phone to a colleague in London, somehow sketching the ice formations into lucid, poetic prose.
Vidal’s early years were itinerant. He was born in 1949 in Accra, Ghana, to Roland, one of the last civil servants with the colonial office before the country gained independence from the British, and Barbara (née Winter-Evans). When he was young the family moved to Freshwater on the Isle of Wight, where John was sent to a Catholic boarding school. In the holidays he travelled back to Lagos, Nigeria, where his father was posted, before the family moved to Sunderland. John became a lifelong supporter of Sunderland FC.
After studying English and economics at Birmingham University, where he wrote for the student newspaper and shared a flat with Ozzy Osbourne, Vidal taught English in Paris and hung around smoking on the Left Bank, ­trying to make it as a writer. He worked for several French newspapers then moved back to Britain to work on a paper in Shropshire.
Evening shifts on the Sunday Mirror in Manchester led to a job as a sub-editor on the arts desk at The Guardian in 1983. At the time he was married to Polly Phillimore, a writer, and was living in a kind of commune in Chelsea, where at any given time a dozen people, invariably artists or activists, lived and cooked on a rota.
Hospitality came ­naturally to him: Vidal often lent money and never asked for it back. He was also spontaneous, once heading back to Paris for a weekend but staying for three months and then bringing back half a dozen French people who moved into the house in exchange for helping him to polish his undercover persona.
After an amicable divorce from Phillimore, Vidal was in a relationship with Jay Griffiths, an environmental author who helped him to write McLibel. When they split up, his friends Adrian Evans (the theatre producer) and ­Bettany Hughes (the TV historian) invited him to stay in their spare room in west London. The arrangement worked so well he ended up living there for ten years.
Though Vidal never had children of his own, he became like a ­beloved (if slightly eccentric) uncle to the married couple’s young daughters, returning from his travels bearing gifts such as the tooth of the world’s biggest fish.
His heart, however, remained in Pont-y-blew in Wales, where, with his brother Peter, he renovated a 17th-century iron forge. He loved the idiosyncrasy of the place, and it became akin to a club for many of his friends. Lately he lived there with his second wife, Jen Bates, a photographer and campaigner with Friends of the Earth.
Somewhat incongruously for such a serious-minded journalist, one of his chief pleasures in Pont-y-blew was staging pantos at the local theatre.
John Vidal, journalist, was born on January 5, 1949. He died of prostate cancer on October 19, 2023, aged 74

https://www.thetimes.com/article/tci-fou.title: TCI founder Chris Hohn pays himself £275m dividend
https://www.thetimes.com/article/tci-fou.text:
The billionaire hedge fund tycoon Sir Chris Hohn has awarded himself a £275 million dividend despite a near halving of annual profits at his investment firm.
The $346 million payout from his TCI Fund Management Limited business follows a record $689.6 million dividend distributed by the group a year earlier, which was the biggest ever enjoyed by an individual based in the UK. While this year’s payout is significantly lower after volatile markets knocked TCI’s investment performance, Hohn nevertheless remains in the top ranks of Britain’s best-paid business figures.
The stockpicker, whose Mayfair-based firm previously employed Rishi Sunak, is the son of a Jamaican car mechanic and has amassed a fortune since setting up his TCI business in 2003.
He is an aggressive activist investor, who has built stakes in companies including Alphabet, the owner of Google, and then agitated for change to improve shareholder returns. He has recently intervened at Airbus, the French planemaker, and in 2017 became embroiled in a boardroom row about who should run the London Stock Exchange Group.
Accounts for Hohn’s hedge fund group show the latest dividend was paid to another business controlled by the tycoon and that the money was “primarily utilised … to invest into an investment fund”. Previous payouts were similarly reinvested.
TCI Fund Management Limited paid a smaller dividend compared with 2022 after its pre-tax profits dropped 48 per cent to $370.9 million in the 12 months to the end of February, on revenues that slid by 41 per cent to $701.2 million. Its turnover fell because of a decline in management and performance fees earned by the business “as a result of the negative investment performance” of the funds it manages, the accounts showed.
Rampant inflation and worries about the war in Ukraine hit markets last year, putting pressure on investors including Hohn. TCI said in its results that its directors “are aware of the challenging financial market conditions but remain optimistic about the future profitability of the company”.
Hohn declined to comment on the dividend.
As well as being regarded as one of Britain’s top investors, Hohn is one of the country’s leading philanthropists and was knighted for his charitable endeavours in 2014.
His charity The Children’s Investment Fund Foundation, which is backed by his hedge fund firm, pledged $491 million to good causes last year and has supported initiatives including measures to tackle child sexual abuse and malnutrition. Hohn is also the biggest individual donor to the Extinction Rebellion climate change campaign group.
He was ranked 42nd in this year’s Sunday Times Rich List with a net worth of £5 billion. He made headlines in 2014 when a court awarded his ex-wife $530 million in one of Britain’s biggest divorce settlements.

image.caption: Sir Chris Hohn has a net worth of £5 billion, according to the Sunday Times Rich List but his $346 million payout this year was down from $689.6 million last year

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Not the End of the World by Hannah Ritchie review — ignore the eco-doomsters
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: Good news: a young data scientist shows we have probably already averted the worst of the climate crisis. By Ben Cooke
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
As the climate crisis has deepened, some activists have decided that the best way to convince people to do something about it is to tell them it will be almost impossible to solve. This questionable strategy has found its loudest exponent in Roger Hallam, the co-founder of Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil.
“The situation is beyond f***ed,” he tweeted in October, adding “1,000s of millions of climate refugees, economic collapse and human extinction. Only mass civil resistance can stop the top global one per cent imposing mass death on billions of people.”
Hallam’s theory of persuasion is simple: he thinks that if he can terrify people enough, they will rush to join him at the barricades. But how many people actually think this way? How many people, when told they will die if they don’t join Extinction Rebellion, think, “Time to crack out the superglue”? How many, feeling that a global revolution just isn’t going to happen, fall back on passivity?
I’d wager that far more people fall into the latter camp. That’s not to say that Extinction Rebellion’s efforts have been counterproductive, it’s just that Hallam’s insistence on the need for a global revolution is unnecessarily depressing. It ignores the progress we have already made without one — the progress in which Extinction Rebellion has played a big part. And in so doing, it saps the resolve we need to progress further.
In Not the End of the World, Hannah Ritchie expounds a different theory of persuasion: if you show people the progress that has been made on environmental problems, you will inspire them to help to finish the job. As well as being a more plausible reading of human nature, this thesis has another advantage over Hallam’s lurid prediction of human extinction: it’s based in fact.
Over the past few years, while still in her twenties, Ritchie has made a name for herself in sustainability circles by using data to tell a surprisingly optimistic story about the planet’s future. As the head of research at the website Our World in Data, she has shown that on a number of indices — air pollution, climate change, deforestation, overfishing and biodiversity loss — humanity is beginning to abandon its dirty habits. Not the End of the World is her synthesis: it’s a riposte to the apocalyptic bloviation of Hallam and others.
“I don’t think we’re going to be the last generation,” she writes. “I think we could be the first generation. We have the opportunity to be the first generation that leaves the environment in a better state than we found it.”
• The Climate Book by Greta Thunberg: a crash course in saving the planet
At least as far as climate change is concerned, this is a tad Pollyanna-ish. No matter what we do now the climate at the end of the 21st century will be less hospitable than it was at its beginning. But this overstatement should not detract too much from the thrust of her message, which is that we have probably already averted the worst of climate change.
Before the2015 Paris climate accords, the world seemed set for four or five degrees of warming, which would have been an apocalyptic outcome. Now, thanks to international co-operation, chunky green legislation and the plummeting cost of renewables, we have a good chance of limiting it to two degrees, perhaps less. Carbon emissions peaked per capita in 2012 and should begin to decline in absolute terms before 2030.
Ritchie reports these facts with the gobsmacked relief of someone who once believed the world was coming to an end. She writes that “when I was in my early teens, I thought most of us were going to die from climate change. I tried to convince my classmates, too. For my English oral exam I held up a map of all the cities and coastlines that were going to sink by the end of the century.”
At the same time as ameliorating climate change, we have also begun to solve many of our other environmental problems. In 1900 London’s air was dirtier than that of any city today; it’s now cleaner than it has been in centuries. Between 2013 and 2020 China cut its air pollution by 40 per cent and as a result life expectancy in Beijing increased by 4.6 years. Deforestation rates peaked in the 1980s and have now fallen by more than half. The amount of land used to grow food may have peaked already, and while biodiversity continues to decline, megafauna such as wolves, lynxes and bears are and making a comeback across Europe.
Ritchie’s point is not that there’s nothing to worry about, it’s that we’re making progress and have the chance to make much more. It’s a stark contrast with Hallam’s message, which at least to me seems obviously theological. He seems to pine for a morally purifying cataclysm through which we may finally learn to live as we should — an impulse as old as the Book of Revelation.
In contrast, Ritchie’s message is more prosaic. She says we don’t need a moral transformation to secure our future because we’re already securing it. We just need to speed up. Written in chatty, lucid prose, this is a book for anyone who finds it difficult to believe in a better future. It’s the most uplifting book I’ve read all year.Not the End of the World: How We Can Be the First Generation to Build a Sustainable Planet by Hannah Ritchie (Chatto & Windus, 352pp; £22). https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/arti.title: Why the humble soup is trending
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/arti.text:
Soup is set to be hot again. Yes, sure — soup for autumn is hardly, well, groundbreaking. But six decades after Andy Warhol reproduced a ton of Campbell’s soup tins for pop art’s finest moment, pop culture is embracing it with open, wool-sweatered arms in a whole new way.
The trend is mainly down to a wave of soup lovers shaking up the scene on social media. Search for soup on TikTok and you’re hit with a tsunami of videos: in the past 120 days alone, videos with #soup have been viewed 88 million times in the UK and 8 billion times across the world — that’s roughly one portion per person, plus a few extra ladles. All of them promise easy, healthy, tasty broths to make at home, plus some stodgy hotchpotch hits: French onion pasta, tomato bisque, and lasagne soup, which is, as the name suggests, a kind of semi-liquidised ode to the al forno classic, fawned over by the singer SZA no less.
Indeed a batch of cooler creatives are making soup sexy. One of the best out there is Theresa von Wangenheim, whose account @sssssoupsssss has more than 46,000 followers on Instagram. Von Wangenheim posts an array of deliciously photographed souped-up soups — caviar-topped vichyssoise, verdant greens drizzled with lip-smacking oils and broths topped with fluffy dumplings — as well as the occasional carousel matching her creations to red-carpet looks. “I started it about five years ago as a creative outlet with no clear goal in mind,” she says. “I’ve seen it grow fourfold over the past year, through partnerships and lots of reshares.” Now she runs her own Substack, is featured on the “Depop for food” app Delli and has merchandise including a chic calendar that, ironically, is so popular it’s pretty much always out of stock.
“The soup community is so much fun,” von Wangenheim continues. “I get sent loads of memes, recipe ideas, soup recreations and questions every day. I’ve even made some IRL friends through @sssssoupsssss.” On the topic of memes, they are everywhere: she points to the seasonal reshare of Seinfeld’s I’m Shifting into Soup Mode, but there’s also the much-loved Good Soup clip from Girls.
Another viral moment came from Annie Rauwerda, best known for her wildly popular @depthsofwikipedia Instagram account. Inspired by perpetual stew, an ancient method of making soup where the pot is never entirely emptied, Rauwerda became the self-proclaimed steward of a 60-day broth added to over time by New Yorkers. Sadly the stew kicked the bucket back in August.
So is soup actually in fashion? Earlier in the year, it was added to the menu for the Met Gala in tribute to Karl Lagerfeld, washed down with — of course — a can of Diet Coke. Elsewhere, the soupermodel Salma Hayek claimed that chicken soup “is even more important than skincare” when it comes to beauty routines. “In my biased opinion, soup has always been in fashion, but TikTok and Instagram are definitely helping it feel extra à la mode these days,” von Wangenheim tells me.
• Nine easy and delicious soup recipes from top chefs
It’s easy to see why it’s gaining some momentum now. The cost of living crisis is still fuelling us to make cheaper meals — plus add in the soupy, sentimental Seventies revival pot and you’ve got the perfect recipe for soup fever.
But could it have a more important role to play in our silly little lives? After all, it became a symbol of protest last year through Just Stop Oil splattering Van Gogh’s Sunflowers with the stuff, going full circle when other climate protesters glued themselves to Warhol’s Campbell’s Soup in Canberra.
OK, perhaps not. Instead, simply enjoy the fact that tomato red – the exact shade of the OG Heinz Cream of Tomato – is the colour to wear right now, as seen on the catwalks of Ferragamo, Gucci and Loewe. Souperb!
The Beet GenerationEnjoy the last licks of blood orange season with this zesty blood orange and beetroot soup.
The Green GiantA lighter vichyssoise (cream-free, and half potato, half celeriac – sue me!), with a fried courgette blossom and tons of herbs because we’re in denial about winter coming.
The Cauliflower DreamSoft-launch autumn with a light but warming cauliflower and squash soup, topped with a drizzle of chilli oil, sesame seeds and spring onions.
You Say TomatoBaked Boursin tomato soup! Haters will call it a sauce rather than a soup, but it’s winter and now is not the time to turn down warm and cosy dishes. Perfect for hibernation.
author: Kyle MacNeill

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/exti.title: Extinction Rebellion co-founder avoids jail over protest damage
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/exti.subtitle: Gail Bradbrook given a suspended sentence after prolonged legal wrangling over £27,000 damage to window on a government building
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/exti.text:
A prominent climate change protester who smashed the window of a government building with a hammer and woodworking tool causing more than £27,000 worth of damage has avoided jail after a lengthy legal battle.
Dr Gail Bradbrook, a co-founder of the group Extinction Rebellion, scaled the entrance canopy of the Department for Transport in Westminster on October 15, 2019, to protest against the government’s proposals for HS2.
In November, the molecular biologist, 51, was found guilty of criminal damage after a trial at Isleworth crown court, west London.
On Monday Bradbrook, of Stroud, Gloucestershire, was sentenced to 15 months in prison suspended for the same period and given a 12-month supervision order. She was also ordered to complete 150 hours of unpaid work in the community within 12 months.
Before being sentenced, Bradbrook, who has represented herself throughout the trial, wept about the impact of climate change and accused the judge of “mansplaining”.
She said: “Where are the killers in the court? Where is the justice in the court system? We can’t see it so I am compelled to act. I maintain that my actions were logical and proportionate and that an absolute discharge is appropriate. I am not a criminal.”
Outside, she was supported by a small group of protesters some of whom were dressed as suffragettes. Also part of the group was Jerome Flynn, the actor and singer currently best known as Bronn in Game of Thrones.
Bradbrook’s conviction follows a lengthy criminal process in which her trial was initially delayed by the pandemic and then abandoned in July last year. This was after she defied an order and used her evidence to bring up arguments the judge had ruled inadmissible, including a 75-page document on her beliefs and wider justifications for breaking the glass.
At sentencing Judge Martin Edmunds KC told Bradbrook that her prosecution was one she “actively sought” and said there was a “high degree of planning and premeditation” in her actions.
“You were helped by another to climb onto a ledge above a doorway to the Department for Transport building in Horseferry Road, London,” he said.
“Once there you attached stickers to the building bearing protest slogans, announced that you were protesting about a range of issues including the climate and the construction of the High Speed 2 rail line, and then used a hammer and bradawl to attack the large pane of security glass that was behind you.”
He added: “It was clearly your intention to commit a crime sufficient to attract the publicity sought from that crime, and to ensure you were arrested and prosecuted.”
Speaking after her conviction in November, Bradbrook said: “I’m at peace with the verdict. The judge gave the jury no choice by directing them that even if I did what I did to protect my own children, that was no defence in law.”

image.caption: Bradbrook placed a sign above the doorway into the Department of Transport during an Extinction Rebellion protest in London in 2019 before taking a hammer and bradawl to the window behind her
Gail Bradbrook outside Isleworth crown court on Monday with supporters, some of whom dressed as suffragettes

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/cait.title: It’s the Celebrity Watch awards 2023
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/cait.text:
The thing is, right — and I know none of us feels this right now — but 2023 was … relatively normal.
I know there were two wars, and Nigel Farage ate a camel’s anus on ITV1 while making a political comeback, and Taylor Swift’s cat — her cat — was revealed to be worth $97 million. And that, of all people, Phillip Schofield, The Safe King of Light Entertainment, briefly became the most controversial man in Britain. Plus: a coronation! We actually coronated a whole man, live, on TV.
But it’s all relative, isn’t it? Like, we had the same prime minister for an entire year — and that’s not nothing these days. It’s a total treat, really. Because, from a constitutional point alone, “Who is the prime minister?” can’t be a question as tricky as “Name all the members of Sugababes” — especially when none of the prime ministers involved ever did anything as good as Push the Button. You can only really have that kind of turnover of personnel when you’re as funky as Mutya, Keisha, Siobhan, Heidi, Amelle and/or Jade.
So, as we pack 2023 into our Precious Golden Memories box — as we coil up the coronation bunting on which King Charles looked inexplicably sad; pop in our bitcoins; wedge in a bottle of Heinz’s thoroughly rebuffed new invention, hot cross bun-flavoured mayonnaise and remind ourselves that the president of Mexico, 69-year-old Andrés Manuel López Obrador, posted a picture on Twitter in February of what he claimed was an elf (“I share [a] photo taken three days ago, apparently of an alux” he wrote, accompanying what appeared to be a picture of Lady Gaga having a nervo up a tree) — let us finish off this still, despite all that, relatively normal year with the Celebrity Watch awards 2023.
Let’s start with: the coronation.
Let me take you back to when our new, old King was crowned on that rainy day in May. Rain, which, as an index of the public’s narrative on the whole affair, was widely agreed on Twitter to have been “sent” by Princess Diana, as “revenge”.
Across the country, thousands of Argos £49.99 marquees stood in front gardens — £7.99 Ryman’s coronation bunting funnelling raindrops across King Charles’s face and onto the sodden buffet tables below. Twenty million people had their televisions on — some from 8.30am, when the coverage started, and early guests such as Emma Thompson, Ant and Dec and some Dimblebys turned up at Westminster Abbey. All having presumably wisely dehydrated themselves in the knowledge they wouldn’t be let back out and allowed to use the toilets until the whole thing ended at 1pm.
As most of the public had never seen a coronation before — Queen Elizabeth’s having happened in 1953 — there was a general sense of curiosity: what happens at a coronation? And, more importantly, who would win it?
• King Charles and Queen Camilla’s coronation — as it happened
There were definitely several clashing narratives. The King — looking at all times rather sombre and slightly overwhelmed — had to deal with a great deal of Tradition. As you might remember, this involved a vast amount of accessories and props: Charles, wearing what appeared to be a solid gold dress (“This represents simplicity,”Huw Edwards, pre-scandal, breathed, somewhat paradoxically), took on board the bracelets of sincerity and wisdom, the sovereign’s orb, the ring of kingly dignity and the rod of equity and mercy.
By the time what appeared to be the oven glove of God turned up, the whole thing appeared to have turned into a game of royal Buckaroo! — or Double or Drop on Crackerjack, where kids had to hold an increasing load of prizes and cabbages until their arms gave way and they dropped the lot.
I was often reminded of the old showbiz gossip about Wendy Richard who, allegedly, when playing Pauline Fowler, refused to do “prop work” if she also had dialogue. If the script said “Pauline irons while discussing Michelle” she would refuse to iron while talking, because she said it distracted her from remembering her lines. Looking at Charles struggling to hold both a royal stick and a magic beach ball while speaking in Latin, I mused: he should have got Richard’s agent.
On the day, Penny Mordaunt seemed to be the clear “winner” of the coronation: you may recall social media going nuts when she rocked up in some custom-made Star Wars queen of the galactic senate (springwear range) outfit. In teal and gold, Mordaunt held a gigantic sword aloft with Bafta-winning majesty and, surely, prompted a whole new series of searches on Pornhub from right-wing men with niche crumpet-taste: “lord president of the privy council own sword bosoms stoic phwoar”. On the day, her odds on becoming the next leader of the Conservative Party were slashed by Ladbrokes from 8-1 to 13-2.
• How Penny Mordaunt became a star of the coronation
But, as we can see now from the vantage point of December, Mordaunt never really capitalised on her moment: what should have been a summer and autumn of “turning up to places still carrying a massive sword but in a casual way” didn’t materialise. Mordaunt’s Coronation Slot turned out to be a bit like Status Quo at Live Aid: amazing at the time, but not really remembered now.
For it’s Queen at Live Aid we remember — and it was, fittingly, the Queen, as in Queen Camilla, who won the coronation. While her husband looked, understandably, deeply emotional about the whole affair — his mum had died, and his estranged son was a few rows back, being steadfastly ignored by the entire British establishment — Camilla brought her usual, jolly, Jilly Cooper-in-ermine vibe to the whole thing. Charles had struggled at the moment of crowning: the Archbishop of Canterbury sweating as he put the crown on Charles’s head; making two attempts, with the second involving a screwing motion, as if trying to line it up with pre-installed threads on the King’s head.
Camilla, on the other hand, took her crown with the internationally recognised gesture of “careful with my blow-dry, love!” and then beamed at her ladies-in-waiting, who all had equally impressive bouffant hairdos. Once all the coronating had been done, she had the air of a woman whose to-do list now contained only one thing: “Have a fag.” Charles, on the other hand, looked like his to-do list had “be monarch of a crumbling Commonwealth, and head of an increasingly fracturing family, until death” — which is definitely more of a shag.
And so the winner of the 2023 award for who had the best coronation goes to: Queen Camilla. But with an honourable mention to Princess Anne, who, seemingly within minutes of the crowns going on, had taken off her mad royal robes, changed into jodhpurs and was riding a horse down The Mall, happy as a clam. I’m pretty sure her agent arranged that. You really do need a good agent for a coronation.
Moving on now, we turn to another king, of sorts — the king of tech. This year prompted a second new award and it’s …
At first glance, it seems extraordinary that such an award would be necessary. Musk is the on/off richest man in the world. He’s the inspiration for Robert Downey Jr’s Tony Stark in Iron Man. He’s a dope-smoking visionary who dated one of the world’s hottest musicians — Grimes — and who named his space rockets Falcons, after the Millennium Falcon in Star Wars. On paper Elon Musk should be a cool guy. His life is what millions of nerds across the world dream of. As the Emperor of Electric Cars, owner of Twitter/and possible conqueror of Mars, this award should be for what was Elon Musk’s best moment of 2023.
And yet: it’s been a 360 catastrofest for the man social media insists goes under the full name of “Elongated Muskrat”. The lowlights?
1.  “Rapid unscheduled disassembly”. In April there was the coining of a meme, when what everyone else would refer to as “my rocket totally exploded, dude” became, in the careful wording of the SpaceX comms department, a “rapid unscheduled disassembly”, when Musk’s Starship/Super Heavy rocket took off — and then almost instantly came back down again, in pieces.
Even as it headed back towards Earth, internet wags were enjoying the new phrase — “Now I know what to say to my wife when I go off too early on a Friday night,” being the general gist. And Musk became self-meme-ing, when a month later …
• Inside Elon Musk’s mind palace with Walter Isaacson
2. The launch of presidential hopeful Ron DeSantis, on Twitter/X, became an international laughing stock when Twitter/X also kept crashing. It was another rapid unscheduled disassembly. Before the event, Musk had hyped the launch — in which he interviewed DeSantis — as the future of politics: from now on, the vibe seemed to be, every future president would begin their campaign on Twitter/X, bending the knee to the King of the Internet.
By the end of the political car crash, though, one aspect of the future did seem assured: that no future president would ever begin their campaign on Twitter/X. For 20 minutes, the interview suffered feedback, garbled audio and crashes. “Is this still working? Can you hear me?” became the catchphrase of the night: Musk’s $44 billion high-tech baby coming across like two kids with tin cans and a piece of string, trying to talk to each other over a neighbouring hedge. Possibly not unrelatedly …
3. The $44 billion Musk paid for Twitter/X is now looking like an astonishingly bad move from a man who’s supposed to be a business genius. Musk himself valued the social media platform as now being worth just $19 billion. The $25 billion loss is entirely down to Musk himself — firing two thirds of the staff; removing headlines from news reports; removing official “blue tick” marks from Oprah Winfrey, Justin Bieber, Kim Kardashian, Bill Gates, Jay-Z, Beyoncé, Harry Styles, The New York Times, the BBC, Reuters and the Nato chief Jens Stoltenberg — but giving them to any Maga bro willing to cough up $8 a month. Musk had, in the words of Professor Paul Bernal, made a terrible mistake. “He thought he was buying a piece of tech — but what he was actually buying was a community.”
• Elon Musk, Sergey Brin and the love lives of the tech elite
And with the platform — which that community used to hang out in, providing billions of dollars of free content— turning into a confusing, unreliable, vastly more ill-tempered mess, from which advertisers have fled in droves, all Musk is left with now is a $25 billion loss. He doesn’t even have the brand, Twitter, any more — dementedly renaming it X has simply led to a world in which people have to say/type “X”, and then clarify, sighing, “You know — Twitter.”
So, 2023 for Elon Musk was the year we learnt: he ain’t Iron Man, he can’t make a p and he simply has no concept of how, or why, humans like to talk to each other. Unfathomably wealthy and powerful, he has no natural predators: his terrible year has been down to him essentially being a T. rex that’s eaten, in a moment of madness, its own legs.
And so Elon Musk’s Celebrity Watch award in 2023 for Elon Musk’s worst moment has etched on the front: “Elon Musk v Elon Musk: Elon Musk lost”.
Despite X — you know, Twitter — becoming so rickety and unstable, people kept on sayingthings in 2023. Headlines kept happening.
Headlines like August’s gloriously improbable “Joe Pasquale impaled in freak moose antler incident in Skegness” — something which, owing to an accident in a pantomime, actually happened. Similarly, “Paris Hilton’s dog dead at 23” was something that also happened — although quite why a very elderly dog dying was worthy of headlines was never quite explained.
“X Factor star Wagner fears he will be assassinated after getting death threats from people confusing him with murderous Russian mercenary group with the same name,” MailOnline informed us, back in July, in a 1,000 per cent googlewhack of a headline, before going on to deliver welcome news. X Factor’s Wagner had a plan, should the assassination attempt occur: “I am ready for them. I will use my martial arts,” the rotund 66-year-old singer assured us. So I, for one, am not worried any more.
During the coronation, my favourite tweet came from someone who summed up the unspoken thoughts of many. “Seems kind of weird the Queen’s not here. She usually turns up for stuff like this,” which was certainly a more patient take than the other big tweet that went viral: “This has been going on a bit now. I’m sure parts of it could have been an email.”
• Did that really happen? — Caitlin Moran on the coronation
However, one of ITV1’s commentators — the Rev Lucy Winkett, rector of St James’s Church, Piccadilly, ran both of these a close third. At the end of the achingly lengthy ceremony, as the great and good filed out of Westminster Abbey, the ITV1 anchor Julie Etchingham asked, solemnly: “So — what does this all mean?”
After a long and suitably holy pause, the rev replied: “This can’t all not mean something. But — I’m still pondering what that is.”
Back to showbiz land, and the sad death of Paul O’Grady, aka Lily Savage, did at least allow one fabulous anecdote about him to resurface. Older readers may remember a mad reality TV prank show in 2003, in which the thoroughly homosexual Dale Winton “married” the page 3 model Nell McAndrew. O’Grady’s response to this event is one for the ages: “Dale getting married — have you ever heard of anything so ridiculous? I mean, how’s Dale Winton going to get a fanny up his arse?”
However, while it didn’t get much attention at the time — and, to be honest, probably won’t now — my favourite quote of 2023 came from the Channel 4 historian Bettany Hughes, long a favourite of mine for being able to deliver “gossip” from 407BC like it’s salacious breaking news that she’s just overheard in Costa.
Asked in The Observer if she had any life regrets, Hughes, with the deep and dizzying vantage point on life that being an expert on ancient civilisations brings, replied: “There was a pair of electric pink jodhpurs from Jigsaw that were in the sale in 1989 and I didn’t buy them. That’s lived with me.”
As a fellow woman with non-purchasing regrets, it’s a comfort to me to know that even if you are someone with 10,000 years of historical perspective, sometimes it really is a pair of electric pink jodhpurs from Jigsaw in 1989 that defines an era.
As mentioned before this country has got through a lot of prime minsters recently, 2022 being the year when, lucky old us, we had three: Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak.
Obviously, it’s unusual for a stable, established country to have so many recently defenestrated ex-leaders knocking around: there’s not really a template for how we — or, more importantly, they — deal with still having address auto-fill on Amazon default to 10 Downing Street when you’ve suddenly been put out on your arse in a blizzard of negative headlines.
As a consequence, I guess it’s not surprising that our ex-leaders acted a bit … oddly during 2023. To the point that we need to work out which one had the most “wtf” year.
The Right Honourable Boris Johnson first — or “Johnson”, as the Labour MP Thangam Debbonaire insisted on calling him in the Commons in June, clearly believing he had forfeited the courtesy of a “right honourable”. Was she right? 2023 was the year that “Johnson” tried — and eventually failed, after a nationwide pushback — to give his father, Stanley Johnson, a knighthood. The question “Why on earthwould we give Stanley Johnson a knighthood?” had only one answer — “Because he’s Boris Johnson’s dad” — and, to what I’m certain was genuine astonishment from both, this wasn’t seen as quite enough reason.
It was also the year — God, was it only this year?— of the partygate inquiry, where Johnson delivered a massive, waffling 20-minute introduction to himself, only for Bernard Jenkin to caution him that, “You’re giving very long answers and it’s taking longer than we need. And you’re repeating yourself quite a lot.”
Perhaps hearing this as less of an admonishment, and more of a glowing reference for his CV, Johnson went on to accept a rumoured £1 million-a-year column for the Daily Mail plus a forthcoming show on GB News, but allegedly turned down a slot on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! after much deliberation.
In the end, talking balls won out over eating them — and staying in the forgiving arms of showbiz won out over the usual post-prime-ministerly activities such as the UN, charities or think tanks. “Low profile”, “dignity” and “for the public good” — not words and phrases on the tip of Boris Johnson’s tongue, in which respect they now join “the names of all his children”.
But! What a glorious year of achievement, respect and stability it was when compared with our other ex-prime minister at large from 2022: Liz Truss! This was, let us not forget, the year Truss was accused of presiding over “missing” bathrobes and slippers from Chevening — a Chevening where “traces of white powder” were found in the toilets. It was also the year Truss coined her own, self-soothing Buddhist chant: “I was brought down by the left-wing economic establishment” is very much a “Nam-myoho-renge-kyo” for someone convinced they’re being attacked by “the anti-growth establishment” of “Labour, the Lib Dems and the SNP, the militant unions, the vested interests dressed up as think tanks, the talking heads, the Brexit deniers, Extinction Rebellion, people on Twitter and people who take taxis from north London townhouses to the BBC”.
Truss then finished the year by attending the Conservative Party conference, and memorably and guilelessly exclaiming, “We are sitting on 50 years’ worth of sustainable gas. Can you imagine, if we unleash that, what that will mean for households, what that will mean for businesses?” with a straight face.
This, alongside dismissing the whole “Liz Truss v a lettuce” meme with a brittle “I don’t think it’s funny, I just think it’s puerile”, suggests Truss suffers from the one thing most poisonous to British people: no sense of humour.
And so, for doing incalculable damage to Britain’s reputation as “guys who might not be able to pay their mortgages now, but can always take a joke”, Liz Truss wins Celebrity Watch’s worst prime minister from 2022 of 2023!
It’s hard, being super-rich, super-hot and so super-rich it needs to be mentioned twice. The law of averages means you have just as many problems as ugly, poor people — but unlike ugly, poor people, your problems are so high-net-worth, glamorous and unrelatable that you tend to gain another problem: people laughing at your niche misfortunes.
Take Gwyneth Paltrow — present fortune an estimated $250 million. This year she was in court accused of skiing into the retired optometrist Terry Sanderson back in 2016. From the start, the trial was, well … unrelatable. Sanderson was suing Paltrow for $300,000 — a huge sum to most, but a bafflingly small one when one considers that the outfit Paltrow wore on her first day in court probably topped that. Instantly pinterested by thousands of fashionistas on boards called things such as Low Key Rich, Stealth Wealth and Loaded — But Not Rubbing Your Face In It, Paltrow’s cream-coloured cashmere rollnecks, Prada boots and simple leather trousers murmured, “I personally know the Hircus goat this cashmere was harvested from. His name is Samuel.” So different from most people’s court outfits — a 1989 suit from Burton borrowed from an uncle and a sanitary towel in the armpits to soak up the sweat.
• Gwyneth Paltrow: everything you need to know about her ski crash trial
But then, maybe $300,000 was the right amount to sue Paltrow for, as Sanderson’s primary claim was that “after the crash, he is no longer charming”. See! The super-glamorous even commit different crimes to us: Paltrow was basically being accused of having “slalomed the rizz out of an optometrist”. But Sanderson was not the only one who suffered, on that fateful day: “Well, I lost half a day of skiing,” was Paltrow’s quote on being asked how that day had affected her.
In the end — as is often the way of the super-rich and super-hot — Paltrow ended up being lauded for remaining so super-rich and super-hot throughout the trial. The public came to respect her ability to so palpably not give a f***, a not-f***-giving that reached its apogee after Sanderson lost the case, only for Paltrow to bend over him and whisper, “I wish you well”, as she left the courthouse to board her private jet. It was a performance so ice-cold, Paltrow could have made up that half-day of skiing on it. Was it, somehow, awesome? Almost gangsta? Yes. But was it relatable? Not on your nelly.
Far more unrelatable, but in a different way, was the news that broke in August about Beyoncé’s touring lifestyle. In pictures that were rapidly shared across the world, one photographer snapped a pile of backstage flight cases with “BEYONCÉ TOILET SEATS” on the side.
“Beyoncé is such an elite performer she can literally request anything,” “a source” told The Sun. “Her team makes great effort to ensure she has her own comforts and a personal toilet seat happens to be one.”
• Read our review: Beyoncé: Renaissance tour
With Beyoncé’s Renaissance tour bringing in a rumoured $2.1 billion in ticket this all seems fair enough. A personal toilet seat is but a mere bagatelle. And, indeed, that is the source of the unrelatability: for Beyoncé must be the only person in the world who could be Beyoncé — a genuine phenomenon on a record-breaking tour, in the middle of a career that has redefined pop — and only ask for “a nice lavvy seat” as her post-gig treat.
Beyoncé! Do you not know what men who play stadium gigs ask for? Justin Bieber requests a private jet “on standby”. Justin Timberlake reportedly insists on the entire top floor of a hotel and his own private elevator — plus all doorknobs to be “thoroughly disinfected”. Kevin Hart, bless his problematic heart/apparently jokingly, stipulates, five women between the ages of 21 and 27 “with an athletic/sexy build” at the venue, for one hour before and to stay one hour after. And when Prince began a residency at the O2 in 2007, he asked for a five-bedroom house to be built for him. Although you won’t be surprised to learn that London’s difficult planning regulations nixed this little dream.
For Beyoncé to be so modestas to only want a guaranteed comfy wazz does, unfortunately, make her wholly unrelatable to the rest of us. Beyoncé! You’re wasting being Beyoncé! Let us do it! We’d make them golden toilet seats at the very least.
However, the winner of this year’s most unrelatable problem of 2023came from a story told by Lauren Sánchez — soon to be Mrs Jeff Bezos, and one half of the world’s on/off richest couple. In November we learnt that she had had an extreme reaction when proposed to by Mr Amazon: when he brought out the estimated $500,000 diamond engagement ring, “I blacked out a little,” Ms Sánchez explained.
• They’re engaged! Inside the world of Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sanchez
Obviously, very few of us will have been presented with a diamond so huge we’ve fainted. But for her, this is likely to become a massively problematic medical condition. Let’s face it — if you’re marrying Jeff Bezos, this isn’t the only time you’re likely to be given a massive diamond. If your husband is worth $169 billion, one would presume that diamonds are going to be a massive part of your life: Jeff’s gonna be doling out birthday diamonds, Christmas diamonds and “f*** it — it’s Wednesday” diamonds. You’re gonna be opening that drawer in the kitchen and finding half a dozen diamonds wedged in next to the Sellotape and the nutcracker. Having an allergic reaction to diamonds when you’re married to someone who could literally wipe their arse on a tiara is going to be a massive,but also profoundly unrelatable, problem going forward. Unless Jeff becomes a more humble man, Lauren’s probably going to spend half her adult life unconscious.
But no one will ever, ever feel sorry for her.
This was the year Andrew Tate — the controversial mens’ rights activist and sex-line hustler — was arrested by Romanian police on accusations of human trafficking. Although it was later denied, at the time it seemed the police had finally found the “secret” location Tate was hiding in when he posted a picture of himself eating pizza: the pizza box branding had apparently allowed cops to work out just where Tate was holed up.
• Why is the misogynist Andrew Tate so popular? His young fans speak out
Although Tate was subsequently released from house arrest and is awaiting trial, it did allow Greta Thunberg to tweet, tartly, “this is what happens when you don’t recycle your pizza boxes”.
With a reputation as similarly unfragrant as Tate’s, Prince Andrew was also the subject of apicture that caused a similar amount of “What? What? Why are you posting this mad picture?”
Attempting to disprove accusations against him — of, again, having sex with a trafficked woman: it seems to be the go-to hobby du jour for a certain kind of man! — “acquaintances” of Andrew posed for the photo, which shows a man and a woman in a bathtub, at the site of the alleged incident. One wore a mask of Virginia Giuffre; the other, a mask of Prince Andrew.
For those who remember Vic Reeves and Bob Mortimer’s “Action! Image! Exchange!” sketches — in which the two wore masks (eg of Jimmy Hill) and committed various acts of performance art — the similarity was remarkable. Have I emphasised how mad it was? It was mad.
“Lawyers claim ‘frolicking’ with Duke of York could not happen because there was not enough room,” as The Daily Telegraphput it, next to the extraordinarily insane photo.
Although not volunteering myself as an expert for the prosecution, I would just offer this one, single fact, re: there not “being enough room”: I don’t think there’s a bath in the world small enough to stop a really horny man having sex. If he needed to, a man would bang in a foot spa. Or a cup.
Sexually, men are very “can do”. To be honest, two people banging in an average-sized bath is the most achievable thing I’ve seen this year. But I don’t think I’ve ever seen a weirder newspaper front pageF.
And so the Tiny Bathtub Alibi wins this year’s photo boo-boo award. I hope, in the spirit of things, someone wearing a paper mask of his face comes up to collect it.
Just as William Blake could see the world in just one grain of sand, sometimes things happen in pop culture that allow us — if we let it — to open up a huge new seam of philosophical inquiry.
For instance: this year, “the world’s smallest handbag” went on sale. Measuring just 657 x 200 x 700 micrometres — making it less than 0.03 inches wide — the Microscopic Handbag is even smaller than a grain of salt and can be passed through the eye of a needle. Responding to the absolutely non-existent demand for women to have a handbag that could fit through the eye of a needle.
Or is it a non-existent demand? For, in the end, the handbag sold for $60,000. Sixty thousand dollars! For something that, in even the most mildly adverse of circumstances, one might accidentally inhale! Raising the question: if the emperor’s new clothes hadn’t been invisible, just very, very small, might they actually have been quite a covetable and stylish investment?
On a similar philosophical question is the winner of this year’s Celebrity Watch philosophical conundrum of 2023: Katie Price’s tits. Or, as MailOnlinefirst alerted us: “Katie Price shows off her 16th boob job in a VERY racy body stocking while covering her nipples with duct tape”.
The head-scratcher? Well, if this is Price’s sixteenth breast augmentation — and I believe MailOnline, it would totally keep a count of such things — then we are, are we not, in the realm of the Ship of Theseus? Or, to be vanishingly more current, Trigger’s Broom.
• Katie Price — the implosion of a reality TV star
Price confronts us with what we may term “Trigger’s Tits”: after 16 operations — to, variously, enlarge, reduce, reshape and enlargen once more — does Price have the same breasts she had 20 years ago? Are these the same bold, iconic guys we first saw in 1996, on page 3 ofThe Sun — when she was just 18? Or did these guys only really start to exist — ex-tits, perhaps — when she had her first enlargement operation, at the age of 20? When we talk about Katie Price’s breasts, what are we actually talking about? Are they something with a single, unified history? Or are they, at this point, more an idea? A concept? A dream?
As you may imagine, I have no answer for this — which is why these two ultimately mysterious and unexpectedly profound chesticles are the philosophical conundrum winners of 2023.
So, there it is! The Celebrity Watch awards for 2023! Looking back now, I can see that, at the start of these awards, I did, perhaps, overestimate how not-weird 2023 was after all.
On further consideration, it was all, still, ruddy nuts.
And that’s before we take into consideration Kanye West being banned from Venice for being “too sexy” on a gondola; Prince Harry’s Spare discussing the frostbite on his willy; Gary Lineker’s one-week suspension from the BBC resulting in a Match of the Day that was broadcast with a ghostly absence of pundits; and the Conservatives’ mooted creation of a “common sense tsar” — on the last of which we can safely say, in the light of everything else: it’s far too late for that now!
• Prince Harry’s Spare review — a 400-page therapy session for mystic Harry
So all I can do, as we reel our way into 2024, is leave you with some last, solid, factual information, by way of apology. It’s time for Celebrity Watch’s traditional What Did We Learn This Year?
• According to a paper published in Science in February, dinosaurs had lips.• India’s first lunar mission has cost, in total, £59 million. As New Scientist pointed out,“This is less than half of the inflation-adjusted £149 million budget for the 1995 film Apollo 13, which needed only to depict a mission to the moon.”• Producers of the world-famous Parmigiano Reggiano cheese are fighting fakes — using microchips. Each genuine 1kg parmesan wheel now has a microchip — the size of a grain of salt — injected into its rind, which can be scanned, to confirm legitimacy. For conspiracy theorists who believe vaccines are all a plot by big pharma to inject microchips into humans, the advent of big parma is going to blow their minds.• Rod Stewart’s wife, Penny Lancaster, would not allow the Da Ya Think I’m Sexy? hitmaker to become friends with Donald Trump. “I have a house in Palm Beach, just up the road from Trump,” Stewart told Scottish Field magazine. “I used to go to his Christmas party and the balls he held — but then my wife said ‘no’. There was stuff he was coming out with, what he was saying about women he had known in the past, and Penny said, ‘You’re not going — he’s a disgrace.’”• And, finally: “Dangerous new snake species with forked penis discovered,” ran the headline in Nature. While no David Attenborough, I would suggest that when we consider the discovery of a new snake “with a forked penis”, the first question we must all ask, surely, is:are they sure they’re holding it the right way up?
